Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions
with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks

Runze Chi Email: mr.rzchi@gmail.com Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Ao Chen Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Garnet Kin-Lic Chan Email: gkc1000@gmail.com Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA Affiliation: Marcus Center for Theoretical Chemistry, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA
Abstract

Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of O⁡(N3/2)O(N^{3/2}) on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at U/t=8U/t=8 and 1/81/8 hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.

Devising compact representations of strongly correlated fermionic states is a central challenge in quantum many-body physics. In recent years, neural networks have been explored as flexible variational representations of wavefunctions [3]. To capture the sign structure associated with fermions, it is necessary to incorporate an underlying bias into the neural network ansatz. Some widely used approaches for this thus use the neural network to parametrize determinant or Pfaffian (Gaussian) wavefunctions [23, 24, 5, 27], an ansatz often known as neural network backflow (NNBF). Fermionic tensor network states (TNS) provide an alternative representation of fermionic signs, incorporating them through a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded tensor algebra [8, 19, 25, 21]. Recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of neural-network parametrized TNS (NN-TNS) [9]. Both NNBF and NN-TNS have achieved highly competitive variational energies in challenging fermionic lattice problems [14, 27, 9].

A general Gaussian state requires O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) pairing-matrix elements. However, modern neural architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers naturally produce sitewise features, O⁡(N)O(N) in total. Tensor network states, in contrast, provide a local parametrization compatible with O⁡(N)O(N) features, but their evaluation on large two-dimensional lattices typically relies on approximate contraction. Gaussian tensor network states (GTNS) lie at the intersection of these two families [2, 29, 34], as illustrated in Figure 1(a). Built from local Gaussian tensors, they describe Gaussian states with area-law entanglement. In the current context, the essential feature is that they combine an O⁡(N)O(N) local parametrization with the possibility of efficient exact contraction.

Utilizing the advantages of GTNS, we introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS). Analogous to NN-TNS, neural networks in NN-GPEPS generate configuration-dependent local Gaussian tensors [Fig. 1(b)]. This yields a generally non-Gaussian wavefunction, while preserving the efficient exact contraction structure of GTNS for each amplitude. The ansatz can be systematically improved by increasing the number of virtual fermionic modes as well as the expressivity of the neural network. The amplitude can be exactly computed with O⁡(N3/2)O(N^{3/2}) cost [32] in two dimensions, and generally O⁡(N3−3/p)O(N^{3-3/p}) in p≥2p\geq 2 dimensions. If truncation is allowed, approximate Gaussian boundary contraction can further reduce the cost to O⁡(N)O(N) [29]. We apply the NN-GPEPS ansatz to study the Hubbard model at U/t=8U/t=8 and 1/81/8 hole doping on the 16×416\times 4 and 16×1616\times 16 lattices. There, we achieve results that are competitive with, or improve upon, all prior results in the literature. Further, we show that direct transfer of the optimized parameters to a 32×3232\times 32 lattice also achieves, without further optimization, state-of-the-art variational energies on the larger lattice.

Method.—We consider the repulsive Hubbard model on a periodic lattice of NN sites,

H=−t∑⟨i​j⟩,σ(ci​σ†cj​σ+h.c.)+U∑ini↑ni↓,H=-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}(c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.})+U\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}, (1)

where ci​σ†c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma} creates an electron with spin σ\sigma, ni​σ=ci​σ†​ci​σn_{i\sigma}=c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{i\sigma}, and ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle counts each nearest-neighbor bond once. In this paper, we set t=1t=1 and focus on U=8U=8 at 1/81/8 hole doping.

To approximate its ground state, we introduce a NN-GPEPS ansatz, which takes the form

ψθ​(n)=⟨n|Gθ​(n)⟩,\psi_{\theta}(n)=\langle n|G_{\theta}(n)\rangle, (2)

where |n⟩|n\rangle is an occupation-basis state, and θ\theta represents parameters in the neural network. For each configuration nn, we construct the Gaussian PEPS by contracting the virtual modes of local Gaussian states [19],

|Gθ​(n)⟩=(𝟏phys⊗⟨Ω|)​⨂s|Zs​(n)⟩,|G_{\theta}(n)\rangle=(\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{phys}}\otimes\langle\Omega|)\bigotimes_{s}|Z_{s}(n)\rangle, (3)

where |Zs​(n)⟩|Z_{s}(n)\rangle is a local fermionic Gaussian state containing two physical modes and NvN_{v} virtual modes on each of its four legs. It is specified by m⁡(m−1)/2m(m-1)/2 independent real parameters in a skew-symmetric pairing matrix Zs​(n)Z_{s}(n), with m=2+4​Nvm=2+4N_{v}. The matrix entries specify pair creation amplitudes among the modes at site ss. The identity operator 𝟏phys\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{phys}} acts on the physical modes (leaving them uncontracted), while ⟨Ω|\langle\Omega| contracts neighboring virtual modes through normalized entangled bond states (|00⟩+|11⟩)/2(|00\rangle+|11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}. We generate the independent entries of Zs​(n)Z_{s}(n) using a translation-equivariant CNN with trainable parameters θ\theta and circular padding, which implements the periodic boundary conditions [Fig. 1]. Combined with uniform virtual bonds, this construction encodes lattice translation symmetry directly in the ansatz. The network architecture is given in Appendix B. The full wavefunction |Ψθ⟩|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle is generally non-Gaussian because a different set of local pairing matrices is generated for each configuration.

For each amplitude ψθ​(n)\psi_{\theta}(n), we evaluate the overlap in Eq. (2) by contracting the virtual bonds and projecting the physical modes onto nn. Using the Gaussian overlap identities in Appendix A, we obtain

Mθ​(n)\displaystyle M_{\theta}(n) =n~⋆[⨁sZs​(n)+B]⋆n~,\displaystyle=\tilde{n}\star\left[\bigoplus_{s}Z_{s}(n)+B\right]\star\tilde{n}, (4)
ψθ​(n)\displaystyle\psi_{\theta}(n) =2−b/2PfMθ(n).\displaystyle=2^{-b/2}\operatorname{Pf}M_{\theta}(n).

Here ⨁sZs​(n)\bigoplus_{s}Z_{s}(n) describes the local Gaussian states, while BB is a fixed sparse skew-symmetric matrix representing the virtual bonds. The selection n~\tilde{n} retains all virtual modes and the occupied physical modes of nn and ⋆\star slices the corresponding rows and columns. The number of virtual mode pairs is b=2​N​Nvb=2NN_{v}. Note that, although Mθ​(n)M_{\theta}(n) is sparse in the expanded space of physical and virtual modes, the amplitude is the Pfaffian of a dense matrix on the physical modes: labeling the virtual and occupied physical modes VV and PP, ψθ(n)=2−b/2Pf(MV​V)Pf(MP​P−MP​VMV​V−1MV​P)\psi_{\theta}(n)=2^{-b/2}\operatorname{Pf}(M_{VV})\operatorname{Pf}(M_{PP}-M_{PV}M_{VV}^{-1}M_{VP}).

Nested-dissection Pfaffian elimination exploits the two-dimensional sparsity of Mθ​(n)M_{\theta}(n) to give the exact contraction cost

TTN=O⁡(Nv3​N3/2).T_{\rm TN}=O(N_{v}^{3}N^{3/2}). (5)

The computational cost of the neural network scales as O⁡(N)O(N), and the contraction cost can also be reduced to O⁡(N)O(N) by using approximate boundary contraction [29].

We optimize the neural-network parameters θ\theta by minimizing the variational energy using variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [1]. The automatic differentiation provides the derivatives needed for optimization. We use these derivatives to optimize the parameters with the AdamSR optimizer [4] and the iterative least-squares minimal residual (LSMR) solver [12]. After optimizing the original wavefunction, we impose mirror reflections in the xx and yy directions and spin inversion through a projection over eight symmetry-group elements [26, 5]. The symmetry-projected wavefunction is then further optimized. During training, CNN products use TensorFloat-32 (TF32), while Gaussian tensor network contraction uses single (FP32) or double (FP64) precision. For final-state measurements, we use FP32 for both CNN products and Gaussian tensor network contraction. Optimization and measurement protocols are given in Appendix D.

Why NN-GPEPS?— It seems that NN-GPEPS is simply another way to encode fermionic sign structures in neural wavefunctions, while here we want to explain why it is a much more natural choice compared with NNBF or NN-fPEPS.

In NNBF, the Gaussian state is essentially a long-range correlated state, requiring 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) information to construct the correlation matrix. Nevertheless, the information provided by the output of modern neural networks, either convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or transformers, represents local properties at each site and scales as 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N). The mismatch between 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) and 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) becomes an unfavorable scaling in large systems. It forces one to use 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) neural outputs as a sparse representation of 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) elements in Gaussian states, transformed through simple linear expansions without a clear physical interpretation [5, 15, 14, 27]. In GPEPS, we instead choose the area-law entangled subspace of Gaussian states that requires only local parametrization with 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) elements from neural outputs. This is a much more natural choice than a normal Gaussian state. The 𝒪⁡(N3/2)\mathcal{O}(N^{3/2}) computational cost of GPEPS is also lower than the 𝒪⁡(N3)\mathcal{O}(N^{3}) cost of Gaussian states.

On the other hand, NN-fPEPS requires a favorable amount of 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) information due to area-law entanglement, and it indeed shows great accuracy in small systems where exact contractions are available. Nevertheless, exact contraction of general PEPS in two or more dimensions is exponentially costly. Although approximate contractions with 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) complexity are available, we observe a clear loss of accuracy when these approximate methods are employed. GPEPS, instead, allows exact contractions with 𝒪⁡(N3/2)\mathcal{O}(N^{3/2}) cost due to its Gaussian structure, avoiding the problem of approximate contractions.

Therefore, GPEPS provides favorable 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) information scaling as well as efficient exact contraction, at the cost of reduced expressivity, which can be compensated for by the expressive power of neural networks. NN-GPEPS hence serves as a natural choice to encode fermionic sign structures in fermionic neural wavefunctions.

Amplitude cost.—We first benchmark the contraction of Gaussian tensor networks on periodic L×LL\times L lattices, with N=L2N=L^{2}. We take Nv=3N_{v}=3, giving three virtual fermionic modes on each leg, and evaluate amplitudes for half-filled configurations using Gaussian tensor network contraction on one A100 80GB GPU. Figure 2 compares FP32 Gaussian tensor network contraction with dense determinant and Pfaffian evaluation using fermix [6].

Nested-dissection Pfaffian elimination has a computational cost of O⁡(N3/2)O(N^{3/2}) at fixed NvN_{v}, compared with O⁡(N3)O(N^{3}) for a dense determinant or Pfaffian. The guiding lines in Fig. 2 show these asymptotic scalings. At 32×3232\times 32, Gaussian tensor network contraction has a cost comparable to dense Pfaffian and determinant evaluation, and at 64×6464\times 64 it is roughly an order of magnitude faster than dense Pfaffian and determinant evaluation. The determinant and Pfaffian computations in fermix are highly optimized through customized kernels, while our Gaussian tensor network contraction still has room for further optimization. Thus we can expect the time cost of GPEPS to be reduced in the future. Appendix C further separates the CNN and contraction costs in a complete amplitude evaluation and compares FP32 and FP64 Gaussian tensor network contraction times.

Accuracy.—We first benchmark NN-GPEPS on the 16×416\times 4 lattice at U/t=8U/t=8 and 1/81/8 hole doping. We note that this small system size is not expected to show the advantage of the GPEPS Gaussian parametrization, but we study it since it is one where existing backflow parametrizations can work well. The symmetry-projected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 states reach energies per site of −0.765883​(26)-0.765883(26) and −0.766152​(16)-0.766152(16), respectively. The Nv=4N_{v}=4 energy is competitive with previous NNBF and ACE results [22, 14]. A joint zero-variance extrapolation of the two projected trajectories gives −0.7673​(5)-0.7673(5). The optimized states also exhibit pronounced spin-stripe correlations and weak finite-distance pairing. Detailed energy comparisons and correlation functions are presented in Appendix G, while the extrapolation procedure is described in Appendix F.

We next assess the accuracy on the larger 16×1616\times 16 square lattice, where the advantages of the GPEPS can be expected to appear. For each NvN_{v}, we reuse the CNN parameters learned on 16×416\times 4 and continue optimization with the same architecture. The projected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 states reach E/N=−0.759835​(14)E/N=-0.759835(14) and −0.760115​(11)-0.760115(11), respectively. Both energies improve on the earlier variational energies reported in Table 1. The Nv=4N_{v}=4 variational energy is already consistent, within the reported uncertainty, with the MR-nVAFQMC extrapolation [30]. A joint zero-variance extrapolation of the projected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 optimization trajectories gives E0/N=−0.7622​(7)E_{0}/N=-0.7622(7).

To characterize the optimized 16×1616\times 16 states, we measure spin, charge and singlet-pair correlations. We define Cs​(𝐫)=⟨𝐒0⋅𝐒𝐫⟩C_{s}(\mathbf{r})=\langle\mathbf{S}_{0}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle and Cc​(𝐫)=⟨δ​n0​δ​n𝐫⟩C_{c}(\mathbf{r})=\langle\delta n_{0}\delta n_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle, where δ​ni=ni−7/8\delta n_{i}=n_{i}-7/8. The structure factors are S⁡(𝐤)=∑𝐫ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​Cs​(𝐫)S(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}C_{s}(\mathbf{r}) and Nc​(𝐤)=∑𝐫ei​𝐤⋅𝐫​Cc​(𝐫)N_{c}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}C_{c}(\mathbf{r}), and the figures show these divided by NN. For pairing, we use the normalized nearest-neighbor singlet Bi​j†=(ci↑†​cj↓†−ci↓†​cj↑†)/2B^{\dagger}_{ij}=(c^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{j\downarrow}-c^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}c^{\dagger}_{j\uparrow})/\sqrt{2} to define

Δi†\displaystyle\Delta_{i}^{\dagger} =14​∑δ=±x^,±y^fδ​Bi,i+δ†,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}\sum_{\delta=\pm\hat{x},\pm\hat{y}}f_{\delta}B^{\dagger}_{i,i+\delta}, (6)
Cp​(𝐫)\displaystyle C_{p}(\mathbf{r}) =⟨Δ0†​Δ𝐫⟩−𝒩0,𝐫,\displaystyle=\langle\Delta_{0}^{\dagger}\Delta_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle-\mathcal{N}_{0,\mathbf{r}},

where f±x^=1f_{\pm\hat{x}}=1 and f±y^=−1f_{\pm\hat{y}}=-1. The term 𝒩0,𝐫\mathcal{N}_{0,\mathbf{r}} removes the disconnected products ⟨c†​c⟩​⟨c†​c⟩\langle c^{\dagger}c\rangle\langle c^{\dagger}c\rangle in the Wick decomposition of ⟨Δ0†​Δ𝐫⟩\langle\Delta_{0}^{\dagger}\Delta_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle. We define ΔSC2\Delta_{\rm SC}^{2} as the mean of Cp​(𝐫)C_{p}(\mathbf{r}) over d⁡(𝐫)≥dmax/2d(\mathbf{r})\geq d_{\max}/2, where d⁡(𝐫)d(\mathbf{r}) is the shortest Euclidean distance under periodic boundary conditions and dmaxd_{\max} is its maximum over all lattice displacements.

Figure 3 resolves the stripe pattern in the projected Nv=4N_{v}=4 state. The real-space spin correlations have a modulated antiferromagnetic envelope, with peaks in S⁡(kx,π)S(k_{x},\pi) at kx=π±π/8k_{x}=\pi\pm\pi/8 and in Nc​(kx,0)N_{c}(k_{x},0) at kx=±π/4k_{x}=\pm\pi/4. These spin and charge periods of 16 and 8 are consistent with the filled stripes found in previous studies [36, 28, 30]. Averaging the spin structure factor over 𝒬={(π±π/8,π),(π,π±π/8)}\mathcal{Q}=\{(\pi\pm\pi/8,\pi),(\pi,\pi\pm\pi/8)\} gives Mstr2=14​N​∑𝐐∈𝒬S⁡(𝐐)=0.013725​(10)M_{\rm str}^{2}=\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{\mathbf{Q}\in\mathcal{Q}}S(\mathbf{Q})=0.013725(10). The stripe strength is comparable to that found with MR-nVAFQMC [30].

Pair correlations decrease rapidly with distance but retain a small positive mean, ΔSC2=1.37​(20)×10−4\Delta_{\rm SC}^{2}=1.37(20)\times 10^{-4}, over r≥4​2r\geq 4\sqrt{2}. MR-nVAFQMC finds the same distant-window measure compatible with zero [30], while HFPS finds long-distance pairing correlations nearly zero within statistical uncertainties [28]. The resolved finite-size signal here does not establish superconducting long-range order, which requires scaling to larger lattices. The Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 states show similar qualitative stripe and pairing behavior on each lattice (Appendix G).

Parameter transfer to the 32×3232\times 32 lattice.—Finally, we test a direct transfer from the 16×1616\times 16 to 32×3232\times 32 lattice using the unprojected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 states. We reuse the learned CNN parameters without further optimization and evaluate each state without and with the symmetry projection. Both sampling and evaluation use FP32 (Appendix E). The transferred states give energies per site of −0.757451​(21)-0.757451(21) and −0.758019​(22)-0.758019(22), respectively. Applying the projection at evaluation lowers the energies to −0.758414​(27)-0.758414(27) and −0.758727​(33)-0.758727(33), with variances per site of 0.01647​(64)0.01647(64) and 0.01606​(82)0.01606(82). All four energies lie substantially below the SCALE and SCALE+GFMC values and are comparable to the MR-nVAFQMC (including extrapolation) results, within their large uncertainty [14, 30]. This improvement is obtained without enlarging the network or performing an optimization at the target size. The projected transferred states retain variance densities comparable to those on 16×1616\times 16, providing a useful starting point for further optimization.

Conclusion and discussion.—We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states for strongly correlated fermions. The Gaussian tensor-network structure enables exact amplitude evaluation with O⁡(N3/2)O(N^{3/2}) cost in two dimensions, while neural networks make the local tensors depend on the occupation configuration. For the doped Hubbard model, NN-GPEPS achieves state-of-the-art variational energies on 16×1616\times 16, while direct parameter transfer yields competitive energies on 32×3232\times 32 without further optimization.

The observed accuracy suggests that the local Gaussian parametrization provides an architecture more compatible with neural networks, while retaining efficient exact contraction. These results highlight the close connection between tensor networks and neural-network wavefunctions and provide a practical route to scalable studies of strongly correlated fermions and their phase diagrams.

Appendix A Gaussian tensor network contraction

An even fermionic Gaussian state in pairing form is

|ΨZ⟩=exp⁡(∑a<bZa​b​ca†​cb†)​|0⟩=∏a<b(1+Za​b​ca†​cb†)​|0⟩|\Psi_{Z}\rangle=\exp\left(\sum_{a<b}Z_{ab}\,c^{\dagger}_{a}c^{\dagger}_{b}\right)|0\rangle=\prod_{a<b}(1+Z_{ab}c^{\dagger}_{a}c^{\dagger}_{b})|0\rangle (7)

where the summation covers all mm fermionic modes, and ZZ is a skew-symmetric m×mm\times m matrix. The state is unnormalized, with vacuum amplitude ⟨0|ΨZ⟩=1\langle 0|\Psi_{Z}\rangle=1. For an input basis state nIn_{I}, its wavefunction amplitude is

ψZ​(nI)=⟨nI|ΨZ⟩=Pf⁡(nI⋆Z⋆nI),\psi_{Z}(n_{I})=\langle n_{I}|\Psi_{Z}\rangle=\operatorname{Pf}(n_{I}\star Z\star n_{I}), (8)

where nI⋆Zn_{I}\star Z and Z⋆nIZ\star n_{I} slice the rows and columns of ZZ according to the occupied fermionic modes of nIn_{I}, respectively.

A Gaussian tensor-network state is obtained from a product of local Gaussian states by projecting virtual-mode pairs onto maximally entangled states [19]. As illustrated in Fig. A1(a), it can be written as

|Ψ⟩=(𝟏phys⊗⟨Ω|)​|G⟩,|\Psi\rangle=(\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{phys}}\otimes\langle\Omega|)|G\rangle, (9)

where |G⟩|G\rangle is the product of NN local Gaussian states, each parametrized by a skew-symmetric matrix ZsZ_{s},

|G⟩=⨂s=1N|ΨZs⟩=|ΨZ⟩,Z=⨁s=1NZs.|G\rangle=\bigotimes_{s=1}^{N}|\Psi_{Z_{s}}\rangle=|\Psi_{Z}\rangle,\qquad Z=\bigoplus_{s=1}^{N}Z_{s}. (10)

Each site has dd physical modes and NvN_{v} virtual modes on each of four legs, so ZsZ_{s} has dimension d+4​Nvd+4N_{v}, with d=2d=2 for the Hubbard model. The bond state |Ω⟩|\Omega\rangle is a product of maximally entangled virtual pairs (|00⟩p​q+|11⟩p​q)/2(|00\rangle_{pq}+|11\rangle_{pq})/\sqrt{2}. Its bra can be written as

⟨Ω|=2−N​Nv​(⨂(p,q)∈bond⟨11|p​q)​exp⁡(∑a<bBa​b​ca†​cb†).\langle\Omega|=2^{-NN_{v}}\left(\bigotimes_{(p,q)\in\mathrm{bond}}\langle 11|_{pq}\right)\exp\!\left(\sum_{a<b}B_{ab}c_{a}^{\dagger}c_{b}^{\dagger}\right). (11)

The matrix BB has the same dimension N⁡(d+4​Nv)N(d+4N_{v}) as ZZ. Its only nonzero entries are Bp​q=−Bq​p=1B_{pq}=-B_{qp}=1 on each oriented virtual bond (p,q)(p,q). The amplitude of a physical configuration nIn_{I} is

ψ⁡(nI)=⟨nI|Ψ⟩=(⟨nI|⊗⟨Ω|)​|G⟩.\psi(n_{I})=\langle n_{I}|\Psi\rangle=(\langle n_{I}|\otimes\langle\Omega|)|G\rangle. (12)

Substituting Eqs. (10) and (11) into Eq. (12) and applying Eq. (8) gives

ψ⁡(nI)=2−N​Nv​⟨n~I|ΨZ+B⟩=2−N​Nv​Pf⁡[n~I⋆(Z+B)⋆n~I].\psi(n_{I})=2^{-NN_{v}}\langle\tilde{n}_{I}|\Psi_{Z+B}\rangle=2^{-NN_{v}}\operatorname{Pf}\!\left[\tilde{n}_{I}\star(Z+B)\star\tilde{n}_{I}\right]. (13)

Here n~I\tilde{n}_{I} denotes the configuration with physical occupations nIn_{I} and all virtual modes occupied. Reordering physical and virtual modes can introduce a fermionic sign. We use site-major ordering, with (up,left,phys,down,right)(\mathrm{up},\mathrm{left},\mathrm{phys},\mathrm{down},\mathrm{right}) within each site, so moving the nsn_{s} occupied physical modes past two fully occupied virtual legs gives (−1)2​Nv​ns=+1(-1)^{2N_{v}n_{s}}=+1.

The amplitude is obtained by computing the Pfaffian of the sparse matrix M=n~I⋆(Z+B)⋆n~IM=\tilde{n}_{I}\star(Z+B)\star\tilde{n}_{I}. Following a strategy similar to that in Ref. [32], we evaluate this Pfaffian by eliminating modes in pairs from the leaves to the root of the nested-dissection tree in Fig. A1(b,c).

Each tree node corresponds to a lattice region, whose mode indices are divided into CC, eligible for local elimination, and UU, retained for the parent. Eliminating CC from the regional matrix MM yields a reduced matrix MU​UnewM_{UU}^{\mathrm{new}} on UU. With modes ordered as (C,U)(C,U) and MC​CM_{CC} invertible, the Pfaffian Schur identity gives

MU​Unew=MU​U−MU​C​MC​C−1​MC​U,Pf⁡M=Pf⁡MC​C​Pf⁡MU​Unew.M_{UU}^{\mathrm{new}}=M_{UU}-M_{UC}M_{CC}^{-1}M_{CU},\qquad\operatorname{Pf}M=\operatorname{Pf}M_{CC}\,\operatorname{Pf}M_{UU}^{\mathrm{new}}. (14)

For a pair k,r∈Ck,r\in C with pivot a=Mk​r≠0a=M_{kr}\neq 0, Eq. (14) reduces to

Mi​j′\displaystyle M^{\prime}_{ij} =Mi​j−Mi​r​Mk​j−Mi​k​Mr​ja,i,j∈(C∪U)∖{k,r},\displaystyle=M_{ij}-\frac{M_{ir}M_{kj}-M_{ik}M_{rj}}{a},\qquad i,j\in(C\cup U)\setminus\{k,r\}, (15)
Pf⁡M\displaystyle\operatorname{Pf}M =sgn⁡(πk​r)​a​Pf⁡M′.\displaystyle=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi_{kr})\,a\,\operatorname{Pf}M^{\prime}.

Here πk​r\pi_{kr} brings (k,r)(k,r) first in the mode ordering and preserves the order of the remaining modes. To improve numerical stability, we select the largest-magnitude entry within CC for each candidate row and accept a nonzero pivot only if its magnitude is at least uu times the maximum magnitude in the full row over C∪UC\cup U. During elimination, we record the original mode labels in the ordered list 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The full procedure is summarized in Algorithm A.

 

Algorithm A1. Local Pfaffian elimination with threshold pivoting.

 
  • 1:

    Input: MM, index sets CC and UU, threshold 0<u≤10<u\leq 1.

  • 2:

    𝒫←()\mathcal{P}\leftarrow(), ℓ←0\ell\leftarrow 0, σ←1\sigma\leftarrow 1.

  • 3:

    while |C|≥2|C|\geq 2 do

  • 4:

    Find the first k∈Ck\in C for which

  • 5:

    r=arg⁡maxj∈C∖{k}​|Mk​j|,a=Mk​r≠0,r=\arg\max_{j\in C\setminus\{k\}}|M_{kj}|,\qquad a=M_{kr}\neq 0,

  • 6:

    |a|≥u​maxj∈C∪U​|Mk​j||a|\geq u\max_{j\in C\cup U}|M_{kj}|.

    if no such kk exists then break.

    ℓ←ℓ+log⁡|a|\ell\leftarrow\ell+\log|a|, σ←σ​sgn⁡(a)\sigma\leftarrow\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(a).

  • 9:

    Append the original mode labels (k,r)(k,r) to 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

  • 10:

If no admissible pair remains, modes left in CC are delayed to the parent, as in delayed pivoting for sparse multifrontal factorization [10, 11]. The parent then combines its children’s remaining matrices with its assigned entries and repeats Algorithm A. Once all modes are eliminated, ψ⁡(nI)=2−N​Nv​sgn​(π)​∏t=1Kat\psi(n_{I})=2^{-NN_{v}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{t=1}^{K}a_{t}, which we evaluate in signed-log form:

sgn⁡ψ⁡(nI)\displaystyle\operatorname{sgn}\psi(n_{I}) =sgn⁡(π)​∏t=1Ksgn⁡(at),\displaystyle=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{t=1}^{K}\operatorname{sgn}(a_{t}), (16)
log⁡|ψ⁡(nI)|\displaystyle\log|\psi(n_{I})| =∑t=1Klog⁡|at|−N​Nv​log⁡2.\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{K}\log|a_{t}|-NN_{v}\log 2.

Here KK counts the eliminated pairs, and π\pi maps the selected site-major order to 𝒫=(k1,r1,…,kK,rK)\mathcal{P}=(k_{1},r_{1},\ldots,k_{K},r_{K}). Pivot signs and log magnitudes accumulate during elimination, and the permutation parity is applied at the end. With nested-dissection ordering and bounded pivot delays, the contraction requires O⁡(Nv3​N3/2)O(N_{v}^{3}N^{3/2}) work and O⁡(Nv2​N​log⁡N)O(N_{v}^{2}N\log N) storage [13, 32].

Appendix B Neural-network architecture

We generate the Gaussian site matrices with a real-valued residual CNN [16] (Fig. B1). A learned embedding maps each local occupation state to a CC-dimensional feature vector, with the same embedding table used at every site. These features then pass through a sequence of nbn_{\rm b} pre-activation residual blocks [17] built from 3×33\times 3 convolutions with circular padding. Each block applies a parameter-free RMSNorm [35] over all channels and sites, followed by GELU nonlinearities [18] before each convolution [Fig. B1(b)].

The features are rescaled by 1/nb+11/\sqrt{n_{\rm b}+1} before an affine 1×11\times 1 head maps them to the strict upper triangle of Zs​(n,θ)Z_{s}(n;\theta). We keep the channel width equal to the output dimension, C=m⁡(m−1)/2C=m(m-1)/2, where m=d+4​Nvm=d+4N_{v} and d=2d=2. Antisymmetry determines the remaining entries. The network settings are listed in Table B1.

We initialize the embedding table with standard normal entries, use LeCun normal initialization [20] for convolution weights, and set all biases to zero. The last convolution of every residual block is additionally scaled by 0.10.1 (Nv=3N_{v}=3) or 0.020.02 (Nv=4N_{v}=4) at initialization, so that each block starts close to the identity map. All learned maps are shared across sites, so the parameter count is independent of lattice size and the same weights can be transferred between periodic lattices.

Appendix C Runtime benchmarks

C.1 CNN and contraction costs

NN-GPEPS amplitude evaluation consists of constructing a configuration-dependent Gaussian tensor network with the CNN, followed by its contraction. We benchmark the CNN evaluation in TF32, Gaussian tensor network contraction in FP32, and the complete amplitude evaluation on A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs of NERSC Perlmutter. These measurements use the Nv=3N_{v}=3 network of Appendix B, with identical initial weights across lattice sizes and randomly sampled half-filled configurations, without symmetry projection.

We report GPU-synchronized timings per amplitude after compilation and warm-up, using the batch sizes listed in Table C1.

Figure C1 and Table C1 summarize the results. The ratio of CNN time to complete evaluation time decreases from 70%70\% at 8×88\times 8 to 43%43\% at 64×6464\times 64. At the latter size, contraction accounts for the larger contribution and the complete evaluation requires 1.0091.009 ms per amplitude. The contraction times are plotted in Fig. 2.

Table C2 reports the floating-point operation count FF per contraction, the achieved throughput F/tF/t and the model FLOPs utilization MFU=F/(t​P)\mathrm{MFU}=F/(tP), where PP = 19.5 TFLOP/s is the A100’s peak FP32 throughput.

C.2 Single- and double-precision contraction

We next compare FP32 and FP64 Gaussian tensor network contraction times at Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 on the same GPU. To isolate the contraction cost, the site-matrix entries are generated directly with standard deviation 0.50.5 and rounded to FP32 before conversion to either working precision. Both calculations therefore use identical matrix entries and half-filled configurations. All contraction benchmarks use two-site leaves, a pivot threshold of 0.050.05 and 2020 delay slots per child. In the FP32 implementation, global-front updates use FP64 Tensor Cores while the contraction matrices remain stored in FP32. FP32 and FP64 timings use identical inputs and batch sizes and include only the Gaussian tensor-network contraction. Figure C2 and Table C3 show that FP32 is faster throughout the tested range.

Appendix D Optimization and measurements

D.1 Sampling and optimization

We use the mixed Metropolis sampler implemented in Quantax [4], with equal probabilities for nearest-neighbor electron hops and site exchanges. Each update uses 81928192 configurations in a fixed (N↑,N↓)(N_{\uparrow},N_{\downarrow}) sector, separated by 4​N4N proposals per chain. Sampling follows the squared amplitude of the wavefunction being optimized.

We optimize the network with the Quantax implementation of AdamSR [4], with first- and second-moment decay factors μ=0.95\mu=0.95 and β=0.995\beta=0.995, respectively. The associated least-squares problems are solved using an adaptation of Quantax’s LSMR solver [4, 12] with relative tolerance 10−410^{-4}, absolute tolerance 00 and at most 500500 iterations, without an explicit diagonal shift. Local energies entering the gradient are clipped to the sampled mean ±5​σ\pm 5\sigma, where σ\sigma is their sampled standard deviation [15].

We constrain the Euclidean norm of each parameter update [15]. At iteration tt, the proposed update Δ​θt\Delta\theta_{t} is rescaled as

Δ​θt←Ctmax⁡(Ct,‖Δ​θt‖2)​Δ​θt,Ct=C01+max⁡(t−t0,0)/T.\Delta\theta_{t}\leftarrow\frac{C_{t}}{\max(C_{t},\|\Delta\theta_{t}\|_{2})}\,\Delta\theta_{t},\qquad C_{t}=\frac{C_{0}}{1+\max(t-t_{0},0)/T}. (17)

The norm bound remains at C0C_{0} until iteration t0t_{0}, then decreases on the scale TT. Updates whose norms lie below this bound are unchanged. A typical setting is C0=0.5C_{0}=0.5, t0=1000t_{0}=1000 and T=1500T=1500, with tighter norm bounds and adjusted schedules for continued and projected optimization.

D.2 Training and measurements

We first optimize without symmetry projection (U), then continue with the eight-image projection. Table D1 gives the training lengths and contraction settings, using the architectures of Appendix B. CNN products use TF32 during training.

When no pivot passes the relative threshold of Algorithm A, the corresponding modes are delayed and eliminated at the parent node. Because the GPU implementation uses fixed-size arrays, each parent node reserves a fixed number of delay slots for each child; we refer to this number as the delay capacity. A sampled configuration is dropped from the energy and gradient estimates of an update when one of its connected configurations exceeds the delay capacity. All reported energies and correlations are measured at fixed neural parameters with FP32 CNN products and FP32 Gaussian tensor network contraction for both sampling and observable evaluation. Table D2 lists the measurement settings. A configuration whose contraction exceeds the delay capacity is assigned zero amplitude, both when proposed by the sampler and when it enters a local estimator, so that sampling and evaluation refer to the same state and the measured energy is its variational energy. In the reported measurements no configuration exceeded the capacity. Statistical uncertainties are the largest block-jackknife standard errors obtained with blocks of 11, 22, 44 and 88 consecutive measurement batches.

Appendix E Evaluation after weight transfer

We transfer the weights of the unprojected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 networks trained on 16×1616\times 16 with TF32 CNN products to 32×3232\times 32 and measure their energies and local-energy variances. We compare three schemes: FP32 sampling and evaluation, TF32 sampling with FP32 reweighting, and TF32 sampling and evaluation. All three use FP32 Gaussian tensor network contraction.

Table E1 shows similar energies across the three schemes, but TF32 evaluation increases the variance relative to FP32 by a factor of about 2.32.3 for Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44. FP32 reweighting agrees with direct FP32 sampling in both energy and variance.

Let ψ⁡(n)\psi(n) and ψ~​(n)\widetilde{\psi}(n) denote amplitudes evaluated with FP32 and TF32 CNN products. Direct sampling from p⁡(n)∝|ψ⁡(n)|2p(n)\propto|\psi(n)|^{2} gives the usual mean of ElocFP32E_{\rm loc}^{\rm FP32}. Samples from q⁡(n)∝|ψ~​(n)|2q(n)\propto|\widetilde{\psi}(n)|^{2} instead receive importance weights

ri=|ψ⁡(ni)|2|ψ~​(ni)|2,wi=ri∑jrj.r_{i}=\frac{|\psi(n_{i})|^{2}}{|\widetilde{\psi}(n_{i})|^{2}},\qquad w_{i}=\frac{r_{i}}{\sum_{j}r_{j}}. (18)

The sums run over one measurement batch. Averaging the normalized moments over batches gives

E^rw\displaystyle\widehat{E}_{\rm rw} =∑iwi​ElocFP32​(ni)¯,\displaystyle=\overline{\sum_{i}w_{i}E_{\rm loc}^{\rm FP32}(n_{i})}, (19)
σ2^rw\displaystyle\widehat{\sigma^{2}}_{\rm rw} =∑iwi​|ElocFP32​(ni)|2¯−|E^rw|2.\displaystyle=\overline{\sum_{i}w_{i}\left|E_{\rm loc}^{\rm FP32}(n_{i})\right|^{2}}-\left|\widehat{E}_{\rm rw}\right|^{2}.

Here the overbar denotes an equal-weight average over batches, and all local-energy ratios use FP32 amplitudes.

At each NvN_{v}, all schemes use the same source weights, held fixed throughout, and collect 6464 measurement batches of 10241024 configurations, with 4​N4N Metropolis proposals per chain between batches. Each run starts from random configurations and equilibrates for 40​N40N proposals per chain. The FP32 scheme is a separate run, while the two TF32-sampling estimators are evaluated on the same TF32-sampled configurations of one run.

Statistical uncertainties are the largest block-jackknife standard errors obtained with blocks of 11, 22, 44 and 88 consecutive measurement batches.

Numerical errors in amplitude ratios can partly cancel in the mean energy while contributing strongly to its variance. The reported transfer results therefore use FP32 sampling and evaluation. The same importance weights can also enter the means and covariances in SR, allowing TF32 sampling with FP32 local energies during training, although we did not use that here.

Appendix F Extrapolation

We jointly extrapolate the symmetry-projected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 training trajectories on each lattice to zero variance. Each fit uses a window of consecutive updates ending at the last update of each projected trajectory: the final 100, 200 or 400 updates for Nv=3N_{v}=3, and the portion starting at 30, 40, 50, 60 or 70% of the trajectory for Nv=4N_{v}=4. Within each window, we average the training estimates of E/NE/N and σ2/N\sigma^{2}/N over bins of consecutive updates, aligned to the end of the trajectory. Each line in Fig. F(a,b) combines all bins from one Nv=3N_{v}=3 window and one Nv=4N_{v}=4 window, using the same bin size for both. We fit these points to

E/N=ϵ0+a​σ2/NE/N=\epsilon_{0}+a\,\sigma^{2}/N (20)

by orthogonal-distance regression, using errors on both axes estimated within each bin.

We repeat the fit using different training windows and bin sizes (Table F). The reported energy is the mean of the fitted intercepts. Its uncertainty covers the two-standard-error interval of every fit, giving

16×4:\displaystyle 16\times 4: E0/N=−0.7673​(5),\displaystyle E_{0}/N=-0.7673(5), (21)
16×16:\displaystyle 16\times 16: E0/N=−0.7622​(7).\displaystyle E_{0}/N=-0.7622(7).

The energies and variances are the sampled training-window values, with TF32 CNN products. The quoted uncertainties reflect fitting sensitivity within the linear energy–variance model.

Appendix G Additional benchmarks and convergence

G.1 The 16×416\times 4 benchmark

Table G.1 compares energies and local-energy variances on the 16×416\times 4 lattice at U/t=8U/t=8 and 1/81/8 hole doping. The correlation functions below use the definitions given in the main text.

Figure G.1 shows the correlations of the projected Nv=4N_{v}=4 state. The alternating spin correlations have a modulated envelope, and S⁡(kx,π)S(k_{x},\pi) peaks at kx=π±π/8k_{x}=\pi\pm\pi/8, identifying spin stripes with period 16. The charge structure factor has a weaker shoulder near kx=π/4k_{x}=\pi/4, consistent with the stripe pattern. Pair correlations decrease rapidly at short distances and give a far-distance average ΔSC2=8.4​(4)×10−4\Delta_{\rm SC}^{2}=8.4(4)\times 10^{-4}. The stripe therefore displays pronounced spin-stripe correlations together with weak pairing at finite distances, qualitatively consistent with earlier HFPS results [5].

G.2 Convergence with NvN_{v}

We compare energies and observables of the projected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 states at U/t=8U/t=8 and 1/81/8 hole doping. Table G.2 compares training energies and independent FP32 measurements on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice. The correlation measurements follow Appendix D. Since the neural networks also differ in width and depth (Appendix B), the comparison tests the achieved accuracy of the variational states rather than NvN_{v} alone.

Figure G.1 shows the connected pair correlation of Eq. (6) along the cut (x,2)(x,2) on both lattices. In Table G.1, Mstr2M_{\rm str}^{2} averages S⁡(𝐐)/NS(\mathbf{Q})/N over the two wavevectors (π±π/8,π)(\pi\pm\pi/8,\pi) on 16×416\times 4 and the four wavevectors (π±π/8,π)(\pi\pm\pi/8,\pi) and (π,π±π/8)(\pi,\pi\pm\pi/8) on 16×1616\times 16. The pairing measure ΔSC2\Delta_{\rm SC}^{2} averages over all displacements with shortest periodic distance d≥dmax/2d\geq d_{\max}/2, giving cutoffs 17\sqrt{17} and 4​24\sqrt{2}, respectively. Both order parameters Mstr2M_{\rm str}^{2} and ΔSC2\Delta_{\rm SC}^{2} are consistent between the projected Nv=3N_{v}=3 and 44 states.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

We gratefully acknowledge support from our major funders, member institutions, , and all contributors.
